tasks.extracted: Quantitative PET with [11C]DASB and [11C]McN5652, 23 people abstinent from MDMA (mean 97 lifetime exposures, last use a mean of 4.74 months earlier) against 19 who had never used it. Specific distribution volume lower in the MDMA group: occipital cortex -68%, dorsolateral prefrontal -55%, parietal -51%, temporal -48%, hippocampus -40%, thalamus -23%, midbrain -21%, caudate -14%, putamen -13%. Editors' calculation from the printed means and SDs (Hedges g, 95% interval): occipital -2.16 (-2.98 to -1.43), hippocampus -1.26 (-1.96 to -0.62), thalamus -0.62 (-1.26 to -0.01), caudate -0.40 (-1.03 to 0.20). Main effect of group p=0.028 to 0.05 by measure; 15 regional comparisons per measure without correction; the MDMA group used every other drug class far more often and was about 4 years younger.

Binding lower throughout the cerebral cortex and in the hippocampus (p corrected <0.001), occipital -46%; after partial-volume correction occipital -39%, temporal -34%, hippocampus -31%, cingulate -30%, insular -27%, parietal -19%, frontal -17%. tasks.extracted: PET with [11C]DASB in 12 men who had used MDMA on a mean of 244 occasions but not for at least a year (mean 2.74 years), 9 men who used other drugs and never MDMA, and 19 men who used no illicit drugs: no group effect (F=1.22, df 2,36, p=0.31) and no region-by-group interaction (F=0.36, p=0.81). No regional means or intervals are printed. Cortical analysis was restricted to the frontal cortex because of the low signal-to-noise ratio, so the occipital and temporal regions where other studies find the largest differences were not measured, and there was no group of people currently using MDMA.

tasks.locator: Results, 'Serotonin transporter', 1st paragraph; Discussion, 'Serotonin transporter', 3rd paragraph; Table 4
tasks.extracted: Review of molecular imaging to November 2015 (one database, no appraisal of the studies): 16 human transporter studies, of which 14 found a significant reduction, with effect sizes from -0.05 to -2.17; of 10 studies measuring occipital cortex, 6 found their largest reduction there; 3 of 4 found lower hippocampal binding; 11 reported lower thalamic binding but only 3 significantly. The review lists down-regulation or internalization, loss of neurones, lower protein expression and competition from released serotonin as explanations imaging cannot separate.

tasks.locator: Report, p. 2260 (regimen and the squirrel monkeys), p. 2261 (baboons and the two-dose animal), p. 2262 (interspecies scaling), pp. 2262-2263 (closing paragraphs); METHODS section 3.2 is the editors’ protocol, not a page of the report
tasks.extracted: Record of what the retracted report claimed, never evidence about MDMA (METHODS §3.2): squirrel monkeys and baboons given 2 mg/kg three times at 3-hour intervals (subcutaneously and intramuscularly), presented as modelling a regimen used at all-night dance parties. One squirrel monkey died of malignant hyperthermia and one baboon died after two doses, and in each species one further animal received only two doses, so 2 of 10 animals given the regimen died and 2 more did not complete it. The animal that received two doses was reported at 6 weeks with caudate dopamine -65%, DOPAC -77% and dopamine transporter -51%, against serotonin -37%, 5-HIAA -48% and serotonin transporter -40%. The report concluded that people taking repeated doses over several hours risk severe dopaminergic injury and possible parkinsonism later in life, and argued the doses were lower than human doses (1.6 to 2.4 mg/kg) after interspecies scaling.

tasks.locator: Retraction, 1st to 6th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The retraction notice (Science, 12 September 2003): the drug used to treat all but one animal came from a bottle labelled MDMA that contained (+)-methamphetamine. Grounds given: failure to extend the dopamine finding to oral dosing, repeated failures to reproduce it with a new batch of MDMA authenticated by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, then analysis showing that the bottle labelled methamphetamine contained MDMA with no trace of methamphetamine, and that brains frozen from two animals that died shortly after dosing contained methamphetamine and amphetamine with no trace of MDMA or MDA; records showed both bottles were requested on the same date for the same amount (10 g), processed by the supplier on the same day and delivered together with different labels and different batch numbers. The notice does not identify the animal that received MDMA or report its results, states that the serotonin neurotoxicity findings of earlier studies are not called into question, and says the dopamine question in primates remains uncertain.

tasks.locator: Results, 'Dopamine system' with Tables 8, 9 and 10; Discussion, 'Dopamine system'
tasks.extracted: Review of molecular imaging to November 2015 (one database, no appraisal of the included studies): one animal and five human studies of the dopamine system, with no consistent effect in people. Of three dopamine transporter studies, one found striatal binding 13% higher than in polydrug controls (p=0.045, effect size 2.92) and 20% lower in people who had also used amphetamines (p=0.007), which its authors read as an amphetamine effect, and two found no difference; dopamine D2/3 binding and release did not differ in 9 people who had stopped; dopamine-synthesis capacity was 9% higher in the putamen than in drug-naive controls (p=0.021, effect size 1.10) but no different from polydrug controls; a monkey study of the vesicular transporter found nothing.

tasks.locator: Retraction, 6th paragraph (closing sentences)
tasks.extracted: In the retraction notice the authors state that the labelling error does not call into question earlier studies of the serotonin neurotoxic potential of MDMA in several species; that it remains possible that dose regimens in the range of those used by some people, but different from those tested so far, produce dopamine neurotoxicity in primates as they do in rodents; that lasting effects of MDMA on dopaminergic function in humans have recently been reported and some people with a history of MDMA use have developed parkinsonism; and that until the dopamine neurotoxic potential of MDMA in primates can be examined more fully, this possibility remains uncertain. The supporting citations were not read here.

tasks.extracted: PET with [11C]DASB in 49 people with ecstasy confirmed in hair and 50 comparison participants: binding lower throughout the cerebral cortex (17% to 46%) and hippocampus (21%, or 31% after partial-volume correction), unchanged in striatum, pallidum, thalamus and midbrain; the reduction held in those whose hair was negative for methamphetamine and cocaine and was unrelated to brain volume, cortical thickness, hormones, genotype or sex; years of use and maximum dose predicted lower cortical binding (F(2,44)=9.57, p<0.0001). tasks.locator: Discussion, 'Recovery'; Concluding remarks, 'Current knowledge'
tasks.extracted: The review summarizes the field as showing that transporter binding recovers after 40 to 200 days, the 40 days coming from a baboon study in which binding rose in pons, midbrain and hypothalamus but stayed low in cortex, and the 200 days from the cross-sectional extrapolation for the pallidostriatum in a study that found no recovery in neocortex. It then asks whether recovered binding means functionally intact neurones, noting a study in which memory scores stayed low although binding had normalized, and concludes that the cause of any recovery is unknown.

tasks.locator: Discussion, limitations paragraph
